## Investigating EFL students' perceptions of feedback: a comparative study of instructor and ChatGPT-generated responses in academic writing

Amal Aljasser

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Received: 23 February 2025 / Accepted: 30 May 2025 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025

## Abstract

Although there are several studies that examined the use of large language models for providing feedback for writing skills, it remains unclear how students perceive the combination of feedback generated by AI tools and feedback generated by instructor. To address this gap, this study examined perceptions of Saudi English as a  Foreign Language (EFL) learners about the effectiveness of feedback generated by ChatGPT in comparison to instructor's feedback in developing writing skills of these learners. The study employed mixed-method design. The study recruited 112 Saudi EFL learners to participate in an advanced writing course. Their writing assignments were evaluated using two types of feedback (instructor's feedback and ChatGPT's feedback). To elicit their perceptions and preferences, a survey was carried out. Results demonstrated that students felt that the instructor's feedback was more useful than ChatGPT's feedback. On the other hand, ChatGPT's feedback was immediate and accessible. Based on the findings, the study suggested that AI tools need to be used to complement instructor's feedback.

Keywords ChatGPT · ChatGPT's feedback · Instructor feedback · Academic writing · Mixed-methods research

## 1  Introduction

Writing is an essential part of learning a language. However, it is essential to provide accurate feedback to improve writing skills (Yu &amp; Liu, 2021). The advent of technology, especially Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, offers many opportunities in the field of feedback. Currently, feedback given by AI tools in comparison to human feedback is the focus of many studies (Steiss et al., 2024). Using these tools created several opportunities for language instruction such as providing real-time and accessible feedback. These aspects are useful to complement the role of human feedback (Alshahrani &amp; Qureshi, 2024). This is relevant to EFL learners who often need detailed feedback to improve their competencies (Mak, 2021).

Several studies have been conducted to explore the effectiveness of feedback gen -erated by AI tools in different countries (e.g., Banihashem et al., 2024; Er et al., 2024; Escalante et al., 2023; Meyer et al., 2024). Also, some studies have been conducted in the Saudi context (e.g., AlGhamdi, 2024; Almegren et al., 2024; Alshammri, 2024; Alsofyani &amp; Barzanji, 2024 ). These studies reported that AI tools are beneficial in providing feedback. However, there is a gap in research about students' perceptions for both AI and instructors concurrently. The previous studies reported results for each type in isolation. The impact of using both types of feedback on motivation, engagement, and writing performance may be better than using only one type at a time. The current study tries to address this gap by examining how EFL learners perceive the combination of both types of feedback on their writing performance. The study aims to compare the effect of instructor feedback and AI-generated feedback in improving academic writing skills among EFL learners. The study also aims to investigate  learners'  preferences,  motivation,  confidence  and  performance  for  feedback (i.e., instructor versus AI-generated feedback).

## 2  Literature review

## 2.1  The role of feedback in academic writing for EFL learners

Feedback is a crucial factor of language learning, particularly for EFL learners who need to master complex linguistic conventions to achieve proficiency in academic writing. Vygotsky's socio-cultural theory highlights the role of feedback as a scaffold  within  the  learner's  Zone  of  Proximal  Development  (ZPD),  where  feedback can guide students through tasks, they might otherwise find challenging (Vygotsky, 1978). Vygotsky (1978 , p. 86) defined the ZPD as 'the distance between the actual development level as determined by independent problem solving and the level of potential development as determined through problem solving under adult guidance or in collaboration with more capable peer'. Constructivist learning theory further supports feedback as an interactive process wherein learners actively revise and build on their knowledge through reflection and instructor input (Ferris, 2012; Bitchener, 2008).  Historically,  feedback  in  EFL  writing  has  been  largely  instructor-centered, characterized by corrective and formative guidance on student drafts. However, the advancement of AI tools has introduced new feedback channels, especially for lan- guage learners seeking additional revision opportunities. Research on AI tools such as ChatGPT and Grammarly shows that these technologies provide immediate and accessible feedback, allowing students to revise at multiple stages (Guo et al., 2024). Nonetheless, debates continue on whether AI-generated feedback provides the level of detail and personalization that human feedback offers (Solak, 2024; Banihashem et al., 2024).

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Most of the previous studies focused on error correction in L2 writing classes. They offered evidence that students who receive error feedback from teachers improve in accuracy over time (Ferris &amp; Roberts, 2001 ). In addition, feedback is classified into two types: direct and indirect. In the case of direct feedback, the instructor gives the correct form to the students. This type is preferable for low-level-of-proficiency stu -dents who are not able correct themselves (Eslami, 2014). On the other hand, indirect feedback appears when the teacher indicates in some way that an error exists but does not provide the correction, thus leaving it to the student to find it (Eslami, 2014). Scholars pointed out that indirect feedback is preferable for most students, because it engages them in learning and problem solving (Ferris &amp; Roberts, 2001).

Feedback can be provided in a way that is called personalized feedback. According to Koenka and Anderman (2019 , p.15), 'Personalized feedback, or specific, studentcentered information delivered to students about their performance in a motivationally optimal manner, is a vital and feasible strategy that middle school educators can use daily to support their students' learning and motivation.' The use of technology provides learners with opportunities for autonomous and personalized learning (Kazu &amp; Kuvvetli, 2023).

The advent of ChatGPT and other Generative AI tools offers several opportunities for feedback. First, AI tools can be useful for self-improvement. AlGhamdi (2024) investigated the impact of ChatGPT-generated feedback on the writing skills of firstyear computing students. The findings revealed that some students felt that feedback generated by ChatGPT was a catalyst for learning and self-improvement. However, some other respondents expressed concerns about its consistency and personalization.  Second,  feedback  given  by AI  can  be  consistent,  objective,  and  immediate (Pitychoutis,  2024; Teng,  2024). This  can  be  useful  for  students  seeking  to  make rapid improvements. In addition, AI-generated feedback lacks personalization and can result in generic, less specific comments that fail to address specific learner needs (Kostka &amp; Toncelli, 2023; Ho, 2024). Lundberg (2024) stated that AI tools are valuable for surface-level corrections but lack the critical support for tasks that require deeper  engagement with content and structure. Also,  Song  and  Song  (2023)  suggested that AI feedback can enhance confidence in grammar and style adjustments. Despite these benefits, instructors need to be cautious. Polakova and Ivenz ( 2024) highlighted that over-reliance on AI could be a major concern.

## 2.2  AI-Generated feedback in the Saudi and Middle Eastern EFL contexts

AI tools are increasingly integrated in almost all academic institutions in Saudi Arabia  and  Middle  East.  For  example, Al  Mahmud  (2023)  examined  whether  and  to what extent Wordtune helped Saudi students' writing. The results showed that the students in the experimental group who used Wordtune outperformed the students in the control group in the final writing exam. Similarly, Alshammri ( 2024) investigated the experiences and perceptions of Saudi EFL learners using ChatGPT for language writing tasks. The findings showed considerable benefits, including support with con -tent organizing, feedback improvement, and personalized support. However, some worries were raised such as academic dishonesty, overreliance on AI tools, and suspicions about the accuracy of feedback provided by ChatGPT. Similar findings were obtained by Alzahrani and Alotaibi (2024). They found that AI tools are valuable for supporting grammar accuracy and organization. However, these tools should be used to support rather than replace teacher feedback. In addition, Al-Sofi ( 2024) reported the results obtained from a study about the role of ChatGPT in improving writing skills among Saudi undergraduate students. The study found that the students generally preferred feedback given by their instructor for assignments that required critical thinking. They stated that AI tools can be used to provide a feedback for preliminary revisions. This preference was also observed in Alnasser's (2022) study which reported that Saudi students benefited from AI tools for lower-level writing tasks. The students relied on instructor's feedback for assignments that required complex analysis. The same finding was obtained from Alotaibi ( 2023) who found that AI tools were effective in improving linguistic accuracy but not for more complex rhetorical skills. This study aligns with Jamshed et al. (2024), who analyzed Saudi students' attitudes toward AI-assisted learning and found that while students are receptive to AI's support in writing, they express a preference for the contextual depth provided by human feedback.

## 2.2.1  Research questions

- RQ1. How do EFL students perceive the feedback provided by their instructor compared to feedback generated by ChatGPT in improving their academic writing skills?
- RQ2. What is the relative effectiveness of instructor feedback versus AI-generated feedback in enhancing specific aspects of academic writing (e.g., clarity, struc -ture, coherence)?
- RQ3. How do different feedback types (instructor vs. AI) impact students' motivation and confidence in writing academic papers?
- RQ4. What are the key challenges or benefits that students associate with using Chat -GPT for academic feedback?

## 3  Methodology

This study employed a mixed-methods approach to evaluate and compare the effec -tiveness  of  instructor-generated  feedback  versus  ChatGPT  generated  feedback  in improving academic writing skills among EFL undergraduate students. The research combined quantitative and qualitative analyses to capture a comprehensive understanding of students' perceptions and preferences regarding the feedback types. During the time of the study, ChatGPT-4 was the latest version available of ChatGPT.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

Accordingly,  the  comparison  was  between  instructor-generated  feedback  versus ChatGPT-4. The version used in all tasks was ChatGPT-4 to ensure consistency across participants and feedback scenarios.

## 3.1  Participants

The participants in this study were senior EFL students enrolled in the English Language and Translation program at a public university in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The total  number  of  the  participants  was  112. This  number  is  considered  sufficient  in second language research. According to Fraenkel and Wallen (2003, p. 102), 'For descriptive studies, we think a sample with a minimum number of 100 is essential. For correlational studies, a sample of at least 50 is deemed necessary to establish the  existence  of  a  relationship.' At  the  time  of  the  study,  they  were  in  their  final year of undergraduate studies and were considered C2-level English language learners,  according  to  the  Common  European  Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR). These students had completed significant language instruction in their ear -lier academic years, and the advanced writing course, which formed the context of the study, was designed to further develop their academic writing skills in preparation for professional or academic careers. The inclusion of C2-level learners in the study is justified by their advanced comprehension and production capabilities in English, which align with the study's aim to evaluate sophisticated academic feedback mechanisms. Their proficiency enables a more specific analysis of feedback's effectiveness, as these learners can engage with and critique complex linguistic structures and content, reflecting a near-native level of understanding.

## 3.2  The study context

This research was conducted in an online advanced academic writing course. In the course, students were asked to produce a research paper on any topic of their interest. The course was broken down into four primary assignments: The first one was the introduction, the second one was the literature review, the third one was the methodology, and the fourth one was the results and discussion. These assignments were set within a two-week interval where at each stage, the instructor offered guidance and feedback to the students. All the students understood the course requirements and deadlines and the assignments were used for this study to gather information about feedback preferences.

## 3.3  Procedures

The primary goal of this research was to examine student preferences and attitudes toward feedback provided by ChatGPT in comparison with feedback from the instructor.  Two  distinct  feedback  scenarios  were  employed  to  investigate  how  students interacted with and perceived feedback from these different sources. In Scenario 1, students submitted Assignment 1 (the introduction) and Assignment 2 (the literature review) to the instructor who provided feedback generated both from her own evaluation and from ChatGPT. Students were unaware that ChatGPT had been consulted for feedback during these assignments. This combined feedback was designed to explore how students reacted to a mix of AI-generated and instructor-provided comments without knowing the source of the AI input. In Scenario 2, students were explicitly instructed  to  consult  ChatGPT  themselves  for  feedback  on Assignments  3  (methodology) and Assignment 4 (results and discussion) before submitting their work to the instructor. The instructor in this scenario provided her own feedback without consulting ChatGPT later, after the students had already submitted their work and after they had consulted ChatGPT. Unlike in Scenario 1, students were fully aware of ChatGPT's involvement in this scenario as they independently sought feedback from the tool.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

The study spans two semesters, with four sessions per semester. The same instructor was responsible for teaching all 112 students across these semesters, which helped in managing the workload and ensuring consistency in grading and feedback. This course was conducted using Microsoft Teams as the primary digital learning platform. Microsoft Teams supported synchronization of classes in which students can interact with their instructor and get real-time discussions. It also included assignment submission and individualized feedback. In this study, students submitted their assignments as Microsoft Word documents through Microsoft Teams. The instructor provided feedback using a detailed rubric (see Appendices A-D), which was embedded as a comment section within each student's submitted document. This consistency ensured that instructor feedback remained uniform across all assignments and students.

## 3.4  Survey instruments

Survey A and Survey B, administered after the assignments in Scenarios 1 and 2, respectively,  further  examined  students'  responses  to  the  feedback  they  received. Survey A focused on students' experiences with combined feedback from ChatGPT and the instructor, while Survey B focused on the feedback generated by ChatGPT independently. Both surveys included the following: 4-point Likert-scale items ranging from 1 as Strongly Agree and 4 Strongly Disagree; open-ended items to capture qualitative insights into students' feedback preferences. In the following paragraph, a detailed description for each survey will be provided. The choice of a 4-point Likert scale in the surveys is intended to eliminate neutrality, pushing respondents to make a clear decision about their perception of the feedback provided. This method is particularly effective in educational research, where understanding strong leaning and preferences can significantly impact instructional design and feedback delivery. Throughout Scenario1, students filled out Survey-A (see appendix), after completing Assignment 1 and Assignment 2. The survey included three main sections. First, 10 items were asking about the clarity, relevance, usefulness, self-confidence, and acces -sibility. The second section inquired about students' perceptions of the two different types of feedback provided. It is worth noting here, that students were not aware of ChatGPT as an assistive tool for the instructor to provide feedback. Accordingly, to  remind this sense of unknowing, the instructor labeled ChatGPT's feedback as 'overall comments'. On the contrary, in-text comments where the instructor's actual feedback. Similar to Scenario 1, students were required to complete two assignments in Scenario 2. However, in Scenario 2, the feedback provided was on two stages. First, students were to consult ChatGPT for feedback on their assignment; second, students were required to fill out Survey-B (see appendix) comparing their experi -ence of consulting ChatGPT for feedback as opposed to feedback provided by the instructor. feedback from the instructor as in-text comments.

## 3.5  Data collection and analysis

Quantitative data from the Likert-scale responses were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics to explore trends in students' perceptions of feedback across the two scenarios. Comparative analyses were performed to identify shifts in student preferences from the four tasks in Scenario1 and Scenario 2. Qualitative data from the open-ended responses were thematically coded to provide deeper insights into the students' feedback experiences. This analysis helped to highlight students' perceptions of the clarity, usefulness, and emotional impact of the feedback, as well as their preferences for either instructor-provided or ChatGPT-generated feedback. The open-ended questions of the survey were coded through thematic analysis. The thematic analysis technique is most common in analyzing qualitative data (Vaismoradi  et  al.,  2013).  Thematic  analysis  goes  beyond  counting  phrases  or  words  and moves on to identifying patterns, themes, across datasets, describing the phenomenon under investigation (Guest et al., 2012). Thematic analysis, through a process of six phases, creates meaningful patterns to identify unfolded themes emergent from the data (Bernard &amp; Ryan, 2009). These phases are as follows. Phase 1: Becoming Familiar With the Data, in which reading and re-reading of the collected data were conducted, searching for meanings and patterns, until the researcher becomes familiar with the dataset. Phase 2: Generating Initial Codes. Coding was done by labeling relevant words, phrases, sentences, or sections. Phase 3: Searching for Themes, wherein relevant codes are combined into overarching themes. Identifying a theme does not necessarily yield the frequency at which a theme occurs. Phase 4: Reviewing Themes, in which some existing themes can be grouped together; others might be split into subthemes. Phase 5: Defining and Naming Themes. Themes are defined and given names that will provide a full sense of the theme and its importance, going beyond surface meanings of the data. Phase 6: Producing the Report, in which results are reported by integrating themes to convey the story of the data in a clear, concise, and straightforward logical manner.

By employing a mixed-methods approach, the study aimed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the role AI-generated feedback plays in academic writing development and how it compares to traditional instructor feedback in an advanced EFL setting. To answer the first research question, an ANOVA test was conducted. This statistical method was chosen to determine whether there were any significant differences  in  perceived  feedback  effectiveness  across  different  groups  of  partici -pants. It allowed for a comparison of mean scores to identify patterns or discrepancies based on relevant variables such as proficiency level or feedback type.

## 4  Results

## RQ1. How do EFL students perceive the feedback provided by their instructor compared to feedback generated by ChatGPT in improving their academic writing skills?

The results in Table 1 indicate that students generally found the feedback provided by ChatGPT to be clear and relevant, particularly in identifying areas for improvement in their writing. The mean scores for clarity and relevance of feedback were consistently low (indicating strong agreement) across all assignments, with the lowest mean score of 1.03 for relevance in R1-A1 and the highest mean score of 1.64 for clarity in R4-A4. The standard deviations suggest some variability in responses, particularly in later assignments. The feedback was also perceived as useful and timely, with mean scores ranging from 1.21 to 1.44 for usefulness and 1.14 to 1.31 for timeliness. Students found it easy to access and review the feedback, with mean scores around 1.18 to 1.28. However, the feedback felt less personalized, with higher mean scores (1.50 to 1.93) indicating a weaker agreement. The impact on anxiety and self-confidence was moderate, with mean scores around 1.65 to 2.00. The fairness of the feedback was generally well-regarded, with mean scores from 1.17 to 1.60. Interestingly, students found in-text comments from their instructor more helpful than ChatGPT feedback, with a significant difference in mean scores (2.00 for instructor feedback in R1-A1 vs. 1.17 to 1.28 in later assignments). Overall, while ChatGPT feedback was appreciated for its  clarity  and  relevance,  instructor  feedback  was  preferred  for  its depth and personalization. The total of responses is summarized in Table 2.

The results show the mean values, standard deviations, standard errors, and 95% confidence intervals for four different groups (R1-A1, R2-A2, R3-A3, and R4-A4). Group R1-A1 has a mean of 1.48 with a standard deviation of 0.345 and a 95% confidence interval ranging from 1.34 to 1.62. Group R2-A2 has a mean of 1.34 with a standard deviation of 0.352 and a 95% confidence interval ranging from 1.20 to 1.47. Group R3-A3 has a mean of 1.59 with a standard deviation of 0.446 and a 95% confidence interval ranging from 1.42 to 1.76. Finally, Group R4-A4 has a mean of 1.64 with a standard deviation of 0.637 and a 95% confidence interval ranging from 1.40 to 1.89. The F-value for the analysis is 2.40 with a significance level (Sig.) of 0.072, indicating that the differences among the group means are not statistically significant at the 0.05 level.

## 4.1  Qualitative data analysis: teacher vs. AI feedback

The study discussed the output of thematic analysis of the open-ended responses, structured  around  two  main  scenarios:  (1)  where  students  were  unaware  that  the teacher was using ChatGPT (Tasks 1 and 2), and (2) where students independently consulted ChatGPT and received teacher feedback afterward (Tasks 3 and 4).

Students found the feedback helpful due to its specificity in identifying issues such as sentence structure, use of tense, and research questions. Since they believed the feedback was entirely teacher-generated, they appreciated the clear and actionable advice. Many students noted that the feedback, which included both positive reinforcement and constructive criticism, motivated them to improve. Without knowing that AI was involved, they attributed the feedback's effectiveness to the teacher's personal understanding of their needs. Additionally, feedback on how to structure their writing, especially simplifying sentences and improving transitions, was wellreceived.  Students  noted  that  the  suggestions  helped  enhance  the  readability  and overall organization of their papers.

Several students pointed out that the feedback was useful to some extent, however,  it  did  not  come  with  examples  or  reasons  to  support  the  areas  that  needed improvement. For instance, feedback that instructed learners to 'use better transitions' was ambiguous. Feedback was rather broad especially when it came to parts of the paper like the research significance or research delimitations. This is because students requested more specific feedback. Scenario 2: Students Seeking Feedback from ChatGPT Independently for Tasks 3 and 4 Students were happy to receive feedback from both their teacher and ChatGPT. ChatGPT provided a relatively fast and comprehensive set of suggestions for grammar and sentence organization, whereas the teacher's feedback was more specific and task oriented. Most students found the multiple sources of feedback from the two sources quite useful to enhance their writing. In fact, seeking ChatGPT feedback independently made the learners feel that they were more self-directed in their learning process than when they had to work in groups. They enjoyed the ability to get immediate feedback from the AI which they could then compare with their teacher's feedback. In fact, despite the use of ChatGPT, the majority of students stated that they trusted their teacher's feedback more. They considered the teacher's feedback as more accurate in correcting certain aspects of their academic writing particularly in terms of content and organization. In contrast, some students were bothered by the fact that they received feedback from both ChatGPT and their teacher. Although ChatGPT offered many detailed responses quickly, the amount of feedback at times made it hard for students to determine what parts of the text to improve. As noted by students, ChatGPT's feedback was quite general and only addressed general aspects of the research such as grammar and coherence, but it was less effective in addressing methodological and analytical aspects of the research. They observed that ChatGPT was not very helpful in explaining specific academic mistakes.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

## 5  Discussion

RQ1: How do EFL students perceive the feedback provided by their instructor compared to feedback generated by ChatGPT in improving their academic writing skills?

The results of the study show that in general EFL students think that the feedback from their instructor is more individualized and detailed than the feedback from AI. This is because instructor feedback was valued for its comprehensiveness and the instructor's knowledge of each student's learning profile, which is in line with Bitch -ener and Knoch (2010 ) who stated that what makes feedback effective is the fact that it must be specific to the student's needs. Students liked the fact that ChatGPT feed -back was readily available and almost instant, yet the feedback given was specific and helpful. This is in line with Teng (2024) who found that EFL students value the neutrality and ease of access of the AI feedback. The main drawback identified was the absence of personalization in the AI feedback, which is in line with the concerns of Kostka and Toncelli (2023) and Cheng (2024) regarding the fact that the comments from the AI are rather general.

RQ2: What is the relative effectiveness of instructor feedback versus AI-generated feedback in enhancing specific aspects of academic writing (e.g. , clarity , structure , coherence)?

The results show that there are advantages in using instructor and AI-generated feedback to improve different aspects of students' academic writing. The findings revealed that instructor feedback was most effective for revising the general organization and clarity of students' writing, offering extensive and related feedback. This is in line with Ferris' (2012 ) study on the significance of directed feedback in the improvement of students' writing performance. In contrast, the results of the present study revealed that AI feedback was effective in handling basic errors such as grammar and sentence organization and provided the writers with specific and useful suggestions. This is in line with the findings of Guo et al. ( 2024) who opined that ChatGPT and Grammarly, AI tools, are useful in improving students' grammatical and lexical density. Nevertheless, the research presented in Lundberg (2024) and the current study show that AI feedback has the disadvantage of failing to provide solutions to fundamental issues with content and structure.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

## RQ3: How do different feedback types (instructor vs. AI) impact students' motivation and confidence in writing academic papers?

The effect size of instructor feedback was greater than that of AI feedback on stu -dents' motivation and confidence. In this study, students felt more supported, more confident, and less anxious when receiving feedback from their instructor, which pro -vided both positive and negative feedback. This is in line with Song and Song (2023) who found that instructor feedback increases students' confidence and motivation. Although AI feedback was valued for its quickness, it was considered less encouraging and less helpful in decreasing anxiety about the assignments. This is in line with Polakova and Ivenz (2024 ) who pointed out that students require the confirmation of the instructor's feedback for significant assignments.

## RQ4: What are the key challenges or benefits that students associate with using Chat -GPT for academic feedback?

Students found several advantages of using ChatGPT for academic feedback, such as the fact that it is instant, easily accessible, and can give specific and practical sug -gestions on how to improve. This finding is in line with the findings of some of the previous studies (e.g., Al Mahmud, 2023; Alshammri, 2024) who report that AI tools provide beneficial feedback. These tools provide instant and standardized feedback. However, the participants in this study point out that the feedback given by AI tools has some limitations. For example, the feedback provided by AI tools is not very personal in many cases. They state that AI tools provide general feedback. In addition, they state that although ChatGPT is useful in dealing with the basic aspects of the assignment, it is ineffective in treating other aspects like methodology and data analysis. Also, the feedback given by AI tools lack the suitability for the academic context. This finding suggests the finding obtained from Banihashem et al. ( 2024) and Solak (2024). Another issue is the overwhelming nature of feedback given by AI tools. Some of the participants complain that ChatGPT provides a huge amount of feedback which creates a burden among the students.

The lack of personalization can be attributed to the current nature of AI tools that have algorithmic limitations such as the absence of learner-specific data integration. In addition, AI tools have limited contextual awareness, and constrained adaptability to specific writing goals. To address these limitations, future feedback systems could be designed as hybrid models that influence AI's effectiveness while embed -ding mechanisms for instructor input, allowing for adaptive and pedagogically sound feedback experiences.

## 6  Conclusion

This study addresses the gap in research about comparing the effectiveness of feed -back  provided  by  AI  tools  in  comparison  to  feedback  given  by  instructors.  The findings of this study show that there are advantages of implementing AI tools in providing feedback to improve writing skills. However, human feedback is still pref- erable among most of the students. They prefer human feedback because it is more individualized and detailed than the feedback from AI. Feedback given by instructors can match each student's learning profile. The main weakness of feedback given by AI tools is the absence of personalization in the feedback. In addition, it is considered less encouraging and less helpful in decreasing anxiety about the assignments. Regarding the aspects of writing, the study results reveal that instructor feedback is most effective for revising the general organization and clarity of students' writing, offering extensive and related feedback. However, AI tools are more effective in pro -viding feedback for grammar and sentence organization. The study also find that the instructor feedback helps students to be more motivated and self-confident.

## 6.1  Pedagogical implications

Based  on  the  study's  findings,  many  suggestions  can  be  presented  for  language instructors. First, using AI tools in providing feedback for academic writing can be immediate and easily accessible. However, this feedback should be given with the teacher's feedback. As a result, a combination of both AI and instructor feedback can provide a more complete support system for students, which can help them build up their writing skills and confidence. Second, it is not necessary to generate feed -back by AI tools for any student. Some students need careful consideration. In other words, AI tools will provide feedback for all aspects at the same time. This may demotivate the student and feel worried about the writing process.

## 6.2  Limitations and future studies

The study contains several limitations despite its findings. Sample constraints were evident by both a restricted number of senior EFL students at one university and thus the findings might not hold when expanded to other populations. The focus of the study was on advanced learners only; thus, it might not be generalizable to students in  lower  proficiency  levels.  Further  research  should  investigate  how AI-generated feedback works across different educational settings and for various levels of stu -dent proficiency. More knowledge about sustainable pedagogical practices could be gained from exploring how combined AI and instructor feedback impacts writing development over time. Some future work could explore the potential of AI tools to provide more tailored feedback by using adaptive learning algorithms which are based on students' individual needs and learning styles. Another limitation is the use of one AI tool in this study and in particular a specific version of it (i.e., ChatGPT-4). ChatGPT is a general-purpose model that is not specifically optimized for academic writing. Employing a specialized tool (such as Grammarly, Writefull, or Elicit) might have yielded different results, particularly regarding the personalization and precision of the feedback. Future studies can be conducted to compare results obtained from ChatGPT and some other specialized academic AI tools. This could have enriched the discussion by highlighting the unique strengths and limitations of each technology. Additionally, a limitation of the study is using only one version of AI tool which is ChatGPT 4. As we know Large Language Models are evolving rapidly. This factor reduces the conclusions of short-term studies. Thus, future studies can follow a lon-

1 3

gitudinal approach or compare between different AI versions. This will better capture the evolution of AI feedback effectiveness over time.
